prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated by the thousands without Doppler or recoil shifts, bringing optical clocks to uncertainties near one part in 10^18

statement.case_for: I have moved from B038 to B018, and I want to say why in scientific terms and not only because of counting. The magic-wavelength lattice is a clue from nature in the sense I care about: choosing the trapping wavelength so that the light shifts of the two clock states cancel is a physical idea about atomic structure, and it solved a concrete problem, namely how to keep the statistical power of thousands of neutral atoms while having the systematic control of a single trapped particle. That is not the frequency comb, which supplies the ruler (2005), and it is not control of single trapped ions (2012). It has been reproduced with several species in several laboratories (Tokyo, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE), and the clocks now resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres, which has an almost existential flavour, since we are watching spacetime curvature in a tabletop sample. The credit is two names, with the concept and first demonstration with Katori and the accuracy, coherence and many-body clock work with Ye. I would write the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation into the citation so the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is on the page. I do not think we should wait for the redefinition of the second: the demonstrated performance is the discovery, and the metrology bodies decide their own calendar.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is real, and I will not pretend a sceptic's objection fails entirely. Ye's tie to Hall and the comb means the committee must be explicit that his share is the accuracy and many-body clock work, not the comb infrastructure. Olsson's rule that a prize goes to the original experiment and not to a later and better realisation is a fair test and I think Ye passes it only narrowly, since the 1e-18 systematics and the coherence of the many-body ensemble are scientific results about the system and not merely a larger number. Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb and Hg groups remain outside the credit. I also still hold that B038 has more discovery content than B018 and is arguably overdue. I withdraw it as my preferred choice only because the credit cannot be defended as it stands, not because the science weakened.

responses.point: Bernhard pressed that the afterglow localisation, the optical transient and the redshift came from several groups within weeks, so Costa, Frontera and Kulkarni are a choice among many, and that he would want a concrete argument for why this triple and not another.
responses.response: I cannot give that argument, and that is the main reason I have changed my configuration. Costa and Frontera for the BeppoSAX X-ray localisation are clear, but the optical counterpart and redshift step involves van Paradijs, Djorgovski, Kulkarni's group and others, and Bernhard is right that a citation for discovering afterglows would hide an arbitrary boundary that we would then have to defend. I also take his separation of Katori's lattice concept from Ye's accuracy campaign for B018, and I would answer it with the citation wording. I place B038 second among alternatives in case expert reports on attribution make a three-name split defensible.

responses.point: Mark agrees on the science of B038 but does not put it ahead of a candidate with settled credit, because he cannot say from the files who is eligible, and he asks that expert reviewers confirm the clock record before the final ballot.
responses.response: Mark's reasoning on B038 is the same one that has moved me: a mature discovery whose credit is unresolved loses to a result whose credit is settled. I agree with his request for expert confirmation of the 1e-18 uncertainties and the inter-laboratory comparisons before the vote, since I am no judge of the details of a clock budget and neither of us can verify them from these files. I also agree with him against waiting for the redefinition of the second. Because he is a member of Fermi-LAT and has flagged possible recusal if B038 leads, the fact that we now converge on B018 simplifies the procedure.

responses.point: Eva asks whether Ye's role is an original contribution or a better realisation of Katori's idea, and wants the citation to treat the lattice clock as a new type of instrument, with a record in discussion of why Ye's contribution is more than refinement.
responses.response: I think her proposal is right, and it answers the chair's question to me. My own view is that Ye's contribution is the demonstration that a neutral-atom ensemble can be kept coherent long enough, and its systematics controlled well enough, to reach 1e-18 and to see relativistic effects over millimetres. That is new knowledge about the many-body system, not only a smaller error bar. I am less comfortable than she is with the word clean, but I think it is sufficient for the pair, provided the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation.

responses.point: Eva argues that the 2005 prize gave the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize gave control of single quantum systems, while the lattice clock solves a different problem, interrogating thousands of neutral atoms with no Doppler or recoil shift, and that the pending redefinition is a reason to prize it now.
responses.response: This distinction convinces me, and it settles the chair's question on whether the citation can put the difference on the page. In my first round I called the clock a superb instrument whose payoffs were prospective. I now think that undersold the physics: the idea is about light shifts and trapping, and the payoffs are visible already in the millimetre redshift measurements. I would still ask her, as the atomic physicist, to confirm that the many-atom statistical gain and the 1e-18 systematics are the central contribution and not just a larger version of what the ion clocks did.

responses.point: Olle continues to prefer B044, arguing that an unresolved pairing mechanism is no obstacle to recognising a robust phenomenon, as in the cuprates.
responses.response: Olle's cuprate analogy is fair, and I do not claim that mechanism must be solved before a prize. My difficulty is different: for B044 the moire platform is still being reshaped by the TMD systems, the credit omits Cao and Fatemi and the precursor theorists, and the three-name version is contested even inside the table, since Mark floated a two-name variant that Olle rejects. I would revisit B044 in a few years. I would not choose it now over a candidate whose physics and credit are both stable.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, on reading the citation, accepts the magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation as a distinct discovery rather than a sequel to 2005 and 2012
Whether expert reviewers confirm the record uncertainties near 1e-18 and the inter-laboratory comparisons, which I cannot verify from these files
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or the Yb and Hg groups have claims that the two-name credit cannot cover
Whether expert attribution reports could later make a defensible set of names for B038 and bring it back as the lead candidate
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for any shortlisted candidate, including B018. My scientific background in string theory and cosmology touches B004 only remotely, and I have no personal tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names. My supervisor and mentor connections do not bear on this list.
